questions.q: In the Prophet’s time some opponents spoke ill of him and his mission. What response does the article recall?
options: They were forbidden to speak in public
Not quite. The article says: The poet Hassan ibn Thabit was permitted to answer them in words.
They were sent away from the town
Not quite. The article says: The poet Hassan ibn Thabit was permitted to answer them in words.
The poet Hassan ibn Thabit was permitted to answer them in words
Yes. “Words are responded to by words, and not by sword.”
They were punished by the community
Not quite. The article says: The poet Hassan ibn Thabit was permitted to answer them in words.
questions.rationale: “One of the Muslims of the time, Hassan ibn Thabit, was given permission by the Prophet to respond in a literary method to the opponents.”

questions.q: A Hadith speaks of a black spot appearing on the heart after a wrong deed. What happens, according to the article, if a person keeps repeating the wrong without introspection?
options: The person becomes more cautious
Not quite. The article says: The heart gradually becomes insensitive, and truth no longer influences it.
The heart gradually becomes insensitive, and truth no longer influences it
Right. Repentance erases the spot; repetition spreads it.
The spot fades by itself with time
Not quite. The article says: The heart gradually becomes insensitive, and truth no longer influences it.
Others begin to notice the spot
Not quite. The article says: The heart gradually becomes insensitive, and truth no longer influences it.
questions.rationale: “If he keeps committing one bad deed after another and does not introspect… then, gradually, his heart becomes insensitive.”

questions.q: Why does the article insist that a negative thought be turned into a positive one “at the very first instance”?
options: Once it sinks from the conscious into the unconscious mind, it becomes part of the personality and cannot be removed
Well reasoned. Delay hands control away.
Because negative thoughts are forgotten quickly
Not quite. The article says: Once it sinks from the conscious into the unconscious mind, it becomes part of the personality and cannot be removed.
Because positive thoughts come only in the morning
Not quite. The article says: Once it sinks from the conscious into the unconscious mind, it becomes part of the personality and cannot be removed.
Because other people may come to know of it
Not quite. The article says: Once it sinks from the conscious into the unconscious mind, it becomes part of the personality and cannot be removed.
questions.rationale: “If you delay in doing this, the thought will travel into your subconscious mind, and then… enter your unconscious mind… no matter how much you may try to separate it from yourself, you will not succeed.”

questions.q: Man alone has been given full freedom. What, then, is his test?
options: To give up his freedom altogether
Not quite. The article says: To submit to God and live with self-discipline by his own choice, despite that freedom.
To discover how many living beings exist
Not quite. The article says: To submit to God and live with self-discipline by his own choice, despite that freedom.
To submit to God and live with self-discipline by his own choice, despite that freedom
Yes. Every gift carries a responsibility.
To use his freedom to master other creatures
Not quite. The article says: To submit to God and live with self-discipline by his own choice, despite that freedom.
questions.rationale: “The test for man is for him to bow down before God despite the freedom that he enjoys.”

questions.q: The Quran says God will change the evil deeds of some people into good ones (25:70). How does the article explain this?
options: Sincere repentance creates a strong resolve to reform, so the wrong deed becomes a turning point towards good
Exactly. The mistake becomes a starting point.
Good deeds are counted twice
Not quite. The article says: Sincere repentance creates a strong resolve to reform, so the wrong deed becomes a turning point towards good.
Wrong deeds are simply erased from the record
Not quite. The article says: Sincere repentance creates a strong resolve to reform, so the wrong deed becomes a turning point towards good.
People forget what they did
Not quite. The article says: Sincere repentance creates a strong resolve to reform, so the wrong deed becomes a turning point towards good.
questions.rationale: “If he does this, the evil deed that he has done becomes a factor that leads him to goodness.”

questions.q: The chiefs of Makkah offered to make the Prophet their ruler. What does the article learn from his refusal?
options: Rulers must come from outside the town
Not quite. The article says: The real work is to change individuals’ thinking and character, not to seek power.
The offer was not generous enough
Not quite. The article says: The real work is to change individuals’ thinking and character, not to seek power.
Power should be taken only by force
Not quite. The article says: The real work is to change individuals’ thinking and character, not to seek power.
The real work is to change individuals’ thinking and character, not to seek power
Correct. That is the natural sequence.
questions.rationale: “The goal of an Islamic movement is not government or political power. Instead, the real focus… is bringing about change in an individual’s character.”

questions.q: “Man is only the manager of his own person.” What does the article mean by this?
options: A person cannot change himself
Not quite. The article says: A person is responsible for his own faith and just dealings, not for controlling the course of events.
A person should manage only his money
Not quite. The article says: A person is responsible for his own faith and just dealings, not for controlling the course of events.
A person is responsible for his own faith and just dealings, not for controlling the course of events
Well read. History is in God’s hands.
A person should take no interest in others
Not quite. The article says: A person is responsible for his own faith and just dealings, not for controlling the course of events.
questions.rationale: “Man is responsible only for controlling his own self: his principal objectives should be to remain on monotheism and see to it that he is just in all his dealings.”

questions.q: Gravity existed long before Newton described it. What human weakness does this example illustrate?
options: We are afraid of new discoveries
Not quite. The article says: We use countless blessings without trying to understand them or acknowledge their Giver.
We trust books more than experience
Not quite. The article says: We use countless blessings without trying to understand them or acknowledge their Giver.
We forget the names of scientists
Not quite. The article says: We use countless blessings without trying to understand them or acknowledge their Giver.
We use countless blessings without trying to understand them or acknowledge their Giver
Yes. Taking things for granted is a kind of ignorance.
questions.rationale: “Man has a habit of taking things for granted… They avail of all this natural bounty without acknowledging their Giver.”

questions.q: What does the article say makes a supplication (dua) true?
options: It is made only in times of illness
Not quite. The article says: It rises from the depths of the heart, out of realization of God.
It is repeated a fixed number of times
Not quite. The article says: It rises from the depths of the heart, out of realization of God.
It is said in a loud voice
Not quite. The article says: It rises from the depths of the heart, out of realization of God.
It rises from the depths of the heart, out of realization of God
Right. Not mere repetition of memorized words.
questions.rationale: “The true dua is one that is based in and emerges from marifat or God-realization… not simply something that is repeated mechanically on the tongue.”

questions.q: Fasting in Ramazan symbolises a responsible life in this world. What does Eid-ul-Fitr symbolise?
options: The end of all duties for the year
Not quite. The article says: The reward God will give in the Hereafter for a life lived responsibly.
A victory over other communities
Not quite. The article says: The reward God will give in the Hereafter for a life lived responsibly.
The beginning of the harvest
Not quite. The article says: The reward God will give in the Hereafter for a life lived responsibly.
The reward God will give in the Hereafter for a life lived responsibly
Yes. And, shared with neighbours, it becomes a festival of humankind.
questions.rationale: “Eid-ul-Fitr denotes the reward that will be given by God Almighty in the Hereafter in return for our good deeds.”
